meta.title: Inventory cost flow assumptions
meta.summary: Specific identification, average cost, FIFO and LIFO under periodic and perpetual systems, the LIFO reserve, LIFO liquidation, dollar-value LIFO, and choosing a method.

videos.title: Why cost flow assumptions
videos.take: When identical units cost different amounts, a cost flow assumption decides which costs go to COGS

scenes.say: Bluestem bought touring kayaks four times this year at four different costs. It sold 700. Which costs went out the door?

scenes.heading: Touring kayaks, 2027
scenes.say: Bluestem started with 200 kayaks at $400. It bought 300 at $420, 400 at $440 and 100 at $460. That's 1,000 units available, costing $428,000. It sold 700 and has 300 left.

sub: A rule for assigning costs to
scenes.say: Because the kayaks are identical, Bluestem uses a cost flow assumption: a rule for assigning the $428,000 between cost of goods sold and ending inventory. The physical flow of goods doesn't have to match.

scenes.heading: The methods
scenes.say: GAAP allows four: specific identification, average cost, FIFO and LIFO. The objective is the method that most clearly reflects periodic income.

Specific identification tracks each item's actual cost. It suits unique, high-value items, like Bluestem's custom expedition canoes, but lets managers pick which costs to expense, so it's not used for identical goods.

scenes.q: Goods available for sale are split between:
scenes.say: Quick check. Goods available for sale are split between what two things? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, cost of goods sold and ending inventory.

videos.title: Average cost
videos.take: Weighted average (periodic) or moving average (perpetual) spreads costs evenly across units

scenes.say: The simplest compromise: every kayak costs the average.

scenes.heading: Weighted average, periodic
scenes.say: Under weighted average with a periodic system, divide goods available, $428,000, by 1,000 units: $428 each. Ending inventory is 300 times $428, $128,400. Cost of goods sold is $299,600.

In a perpetual system, the average is recomputed after each purchase. That's the moving-average method, and it gives a slightly different answer because sales happen at different averages through the year.
Average cost smooths out price changes. When prices are rising, its cost of goods sold and ending inventory fall between FIFO and LIFO.
It's allowed under both GAAP and IFRS and is common for commodities and fungible goods like Bluestem's aluminum.

scenes.q: Goods available: 500 units costing $11,000. 200 units on hand. Weighted-average ending inventory?
scenes.say: Quick check. Goods available: five hundred units costing eleven thousand dollars. Two hundred units on hand. Weighted-average ending inventory? Pause and pick.

videos.title: FIFO
videos.take: FIFO: oldest costs to COGS, newest costs in ending inventory

scenes.say: First-in, first-out assumes the oldest kayaks are sold first.

scenes.heading: FIFO ending inventory: newest costs
scenes.say: Under FIFO, the 300 kayaks left are the newest: 100 at $460 and 200 at $440. Ending inventory is $134,000. Cost of goods sold is $428,000 less that: $294,000.
A useful fact: FIFO gives the same answer under periodic and perpetual systems, because the oldest costs leave first either way.

scenes.heading: FIFO strengths and weaknesses
rows: Old costs matched with new prices
scenes.say: FIFO's strength is the balance sheet: inventory is close to current cost. Its weakness is the income statement: in rising prices, old, low costs are matched with current revenues, inflating profit with holding gains.
When prices rise, FIFO reports the highest income and so the highest income taxes of the methods.

scenes.q: Beginning 100 units at $10; purchases 100 at $12 and 100 at $14. 150 units sold. FIFO ending inventory?
scenes.say: Quick check. Beginning, a hundred units at ten dollars; purchases, a hundred at twelve and a hundred at fourteen. A hundred fifty sold. FIFO ending inventory? Pause and pick.

videos.title: LIFO
videos.take: LIFO: newest costs to COGS, oldest costs in ending inventory; allowed in the US, not under IFRS

scenes.say: Last-in, first-out assumes the newest kayaks are sold first. Almost no business really works that way. So why use it?

scenes.heading: LIFO periodic ending inventory: oldest costs
scenes.say: Under periodic LIFO, the 300 kayaks left carry the oldest costs: 200 at $400 and 100 at $420, or $122,000. Cost of goods sold is $306,000.
LIFO's argument is matching: current costs are matched against current revenues, so income excludes inventory holding gains.

scenes.heading: Tax effect in rising prices
scenes.say: And taxes. LIFO's cost of goods sold is $12,000 higher than FIFO's, so taxable income is $12,000 lower, saving $3,000 of tax at twenty-five percent.

sub: Use LIFO for tax, use it
scenes.say: The catch: the tax law's LIFO conformity rule requires companies using LIFO for taxes to use it in their financial statements too. And IFRS doesn't allow LIFO at all.

scenes.q: With rising prices, which method gives the lowest net income?
scenes.say: Quick check. With rising prices, which method gives the lowest net income? Pause and pick.

videos.title: The LIFO reserve and LIFO liquidation
videos.take: The LIFO reserve shows the FIFO–LIFO gap; liquidating old layers inflates income

scenes.say: Many LIFO companies keep FIFO records internally. The difference has a name.

scenes.heading: LIFO reserve
scenes.say: The LIFO reserve, or allowance to reduce inventory to LIFO, is the difference between FIFO and LIFO inventory: $12,000 for the touring kayaks. Companies disclose it so analysts can compare with FIFO companies.

scenes.heading: Adjusting the reserve
rows: Allowance to reduce inventory to LIFO
scenes.say: If the reserve rises by $12,000 during the year, the adjustment increases cost of goods sold by $12,000. That's the LIFO effect.
A LIFO liquidation happens when a company sells more than it buys and dips into old layers carrying very low costs. Cost of goods sold falls, and income jumps, with a tax bill attached.

sub: Pools of similar items in dollars,
scenes.say: Dollar-value LIFO reduces liquidation problems by grouping similar items into pools measured in dollars and adjusted for price changes with an index. Most LIFO companies use it.

scenes.q: FIFO inventory $500,000; LIFO reserve $80,000. LIFO inventory?
scenes.say: Quick check. FIFO inventory five hundred thousand; LIFO reserve eighty thousand. LIFO inventory? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Choosing a method
videos.take: Choose on matching, taxes, cash flow and comparability, then apply it consistently

scenes.say: Bluestem's founder wants the method with the best numbers. Sam lays out the trade-offs.

scenes.heading: Touring kayaks: the three results
scenes.say: Side by side: FIFO's cost of goods sold is $294,000, average $299,600, LIFO $306,000. Ending inventory moves the other way.

scenes.heading: Factors to weigh
items: Cash flow: lower taxes under LIFO
scenes.say: Weigh the income and tax effects; cash flow, since LIFO saves tax when prices rise; how current the balance sheet is; comparability with competitors and with IFRS reporters; and bookkeeping cost.
Bluestem chooses FIFO. Its costs aren't rising steadily, it may list in Toronto where LIFO is banned, and FIFO inventory gives lenders a more current balance sheet.

sub: A change of method is a change in
scenes.say: Whatever it chooses, consistency matters. Changing methods later is a change in accounting principle that must be justified as preferable and applied retrospectively. That's in Intermediate Two.

scenes.q: Which method isn't permitted under IFRS?
scenes.say: Quick check. Which method isn't permitted under IFRS? Pause and pick.

case: Bluestem's paddle division has steadily rising costs (about 6% a year) and no plans to list outside the US. FIFO COGS this year would be $1,100,000; LIFO COGS $1,160,000. The tax rate is 25%. The bank's covenant requires net income of at least $500,000; projected income before the method choice is $540,000 under FIFO.
Compute the cash tax saving from LIFO.

Pretax difference 60,000; after-tax 45,000. LIFO income 495,000 (if 540,000 is after-tax FIFO income): below covenant. Tax saving 15,000 a year. Options: negotiate covenant on a FIFO basis (many lenders allow LIFO reserve add-back) and use LIFO for the tax saving; or stay FIFO. Conformity rule requires LIFO in books if used for tax.
exam: Compare FIFO and LIFO in a period of rising prices: effects on COGS, net income, ending inventory, taxes and cash flow.
LIFO: higher COGS, lower income, lower inventory, lower taxes, higher cash; FIFO the reverse. LIFO conformity; IFRS prohibits LIFO.
